checkpoints: A Redis key created by `hmset` on `rl:<clientId>` with no TTL/PEXPIRE ever set on it stays in Redis permanently, regardless of whether the client that owns it ever comes back.

Every distinct, never-before-seen `clientId` produces a brand new hash key, so the total key count in Redis grows with the number of unique identities ever observed over time, not with how many clients are concurrently active.

Churning or one-time client identifiers — rotating mobile session ids, one-off request ids, IPs behind NAT — are what turn this into a real production leak, since each one mints a key that is never reclaimed.

The leak stays invisible in a test suite that reuses only a handful of familiar client ids, because that workload keeps hitting the same small set of keys instead of minting new ones, so Redis memory never appears to grow.
The check-then-decrement token math itself is correct; the bug is purely the missing expiry, not a logic error in how tokens are read, refilled, or spent.

Calling `pexpire(key, ttlMs)` immediately after the `hmset` write lets an idle bucket self-delete from Redis once nobody is using it, bounding total memory to roughly the number of currently-active clients.

The TTL must be set to at least the time it takes the bucket to fully refill (for example twice `capacity / refillPerSec` in milliseconds), otherwise a client that is still genuinely active but pauses briefly between requests could have its key expire mid-use.

When an expired client returns, `checkRate` finds no existing key, so it treats the request as if the client were brand new and issues a full bucket — which is exactly the same behavior a first-time client gets, so correctness is preserved rather than broken by the fix.

Confirming the fix works means seeding the limiter with a large number of distinct synthetic client ids, letting the TTL window pass, and asserting that Redis key count or `used_memory` plateaus at a stable ceiling instead of continuing to climb linearly with the number of ids used.
RabbitMQ only removes a message from a queue once the consumer acknowledges it; until then the message stays in an "unacked" state and the broker can redeliver it if the consumer connection drops.

In the given consumer, `channel.ack(msg)` runs immediately on delivery, before `await fulfillmentService.fulfill(order)` has even started — so the broker marks the message done and deletes it before any real processing has happened.

Because the ack already fired, a thrown error inside `fulfill` or a process crash (OOM, deploy restart) that happens while `fulfill` is still running leaves no unacked copy of the message anywhere, so the order is permanently lost with no chance of redelivery.

This is exactly how RabbitMQ's at-least-once delivery guarantee gets silently downgraded to at-most-once: the guarantee only holds as long as a message is deleted strictly after processing succeeds, never before.
The fix is to move `channel.ack(msg)` to after `fulfillmentService.fulfill(order)` resolves successfully, wrapping the call in a try/catch so the ack only fires on the success path.

On failure, the consumer should call `channel.nack(msg, false, false)` to send the message to a dead-letter exchange, or nack with `requeue: true` for transient failures worth retrying, instead of acking a message that was never actually processed.

Correct behavior can be verified by deliberately throwing inside `fulfill` (or killing the worker) before the ack executes and confirming the message is redelivered to another consumer, or lands in the dead-letter queue, rather than disappearing.

The bug is a data-loss correctness issue, not a style nit, and its severity scales with `prefetch`: a higher prefetch count means more messages can be sitting acked-and-considered-done in memory when the worker crashes, widening the blast radius of lost orders.
A BullMQ `worker.on("failed", ...)` listener fires once for every failed attempt of a job, not only on the final one, so it can run several times across a single job's retry lifecycle.

Pushing to the dead-letter queue unconditionally inside that listener — without comparing `job.attemptsMade` to the job's configured max attempts — dead-letters the job after its very first failure, while BullMQ's own backoff-driven retry is still running independently in the background.

A job configured with `attempts: 3` that fails once and later succeeds still leaves a stale DLQ entry for a failure that ultimately resolved fine, and a job that fails all three times produces three duplicate DLQ entries for what is really one underlying failure.

The fix is to gate the push behind `if (job.attemptsMade >= max)` where `max = job.opts.attempts ?? 1`, so a job only reaches the DLQ once its retries are truly exhausted; before that point the queue is already handling the retry on its own and the listener has nothing useful to do.

A dead-letter queue exists to isolate permanent, poison failures from healthy jobs so they don't clog the queue; dead-lettering a job on its first transient failure defeats that purpose by mixing recoverable blips in with genuinely broken jobs.

If anything downstream consumes the DLQ — an alert, a replay job, a charge — each premature or duplicate entry re-triggers that consumer, so a side effect tied to the job that isn't idempotent can fire more than once for the same underlying failure.

Correct behavior can be verified with two cases: a job that fails a couple of times and then succeeds should never produce a DLQ entry, and a job that fails on every attempt should produce exactly one DLQ entry, added only after the final configured attempt is spent.

Splitting a rate limiter into a separate `redis.get` to read the count and a later `redis.set` to write it back creates a check-then-decrement gap: nothing prevents another request from reading the same stale count in between the two round-trips.

When two concurrent requests both read `remaining === 1` before either one writes, both pass the `remaining <= 0` check and both set the key to `0` — one request that should have been rejected gets through, and the limit is silently exceeded.
A test suite that issues requests sequentially can never expose this bug, because there is no interleaving between separate single-threaded calls — the race only appears under real concurrency.

The underlying fix is to make the whole read-compare-decrement-write sequence a single indivisible operation instead of three separate calls to Redis with the event loop free to interleave other requests in between.

Loading a Lua script once via `redis.script("LOAD", ...)` and invoking it with `redis.evalsha(sha, 1, key, ...)` moves the entire read-decide-write logic onto Redis, which executes Lua scripts single-threaded and atomically, so no other request can slip in between the read and the write.

Storing the counter in a per-instance in-memory map is a second, independent bug: each pod counts requests on its own, so N replicas behind a load balancer let a client through at N times the intended limit — the counter needs to live in one shared Redis key, not per-instance memory.
A non-atomic rate limiter is a correctness blocker, not a nitpick, and should be called out as such and kept separate from smaller nitpicks like a hardcoded TTL that could be a named constant.

Verifying an atomicity fix requires a concurrency test that fires many requests in parallel for the same key and asserts exactly the configured capacity of them succeed, since a sequential test structurally cannot exercise the interleaving window.
GEO keys in Redis are stored as sorted sets scored by a geohash value, so a radius search is a bounding-box scan over that sorted set rather than a separate dedicated spatial index.

`GEOSEARCH ... FROMLONLAT ... BYRADIUS` performs both the bounding-box scan and the distance filtering, including the haversine math, entirely on the server, so pulling every member back to the application and computing distance in a loop duplicates work Redis already does natively.

Fetching every member of a key with `ZRANGE key 0 -1` and then issuing one `GEOPOS` call per member turns a query that should be near-instant into O(n) network round-trips, and because Redis processes commands on a single thread, each extra round-trip adds queuing delay for every other client sharing that Redis instance.

A single key that holds every record regardless of region is both a big key, since it grows unbounded as more data is added, and a hot key, since every read request in the system touches that same key.
On Redis Cluster a key lives in exactly one hash slot, which pins an entire GEO key to a single shard — an oversized global GEO key can never be spread across nodes no matter how large it grows.

The fix for the Cluster and hot-key problem is to partition data into smaller keys scoped to a region or city, sized to a reasonable member count, re-bucketing points near a region boundary as needed so a search still hits only one key.

A thorough PR review separates must-fix correctness and performance issues, such as doing distance filtering in application code instead of in Redis or using an unpartitioned global key, from minor stylistic cleanups, and explains why each issue matters rather than only stating the fix.

Correctness of a server-side radius search can be verified by seeding a handful of known points with GEOADD, running the radius query, and asserting the result set is exactly the points within the given radius sorted by ascending distance, with no manual distance-calculation loop present anywhere in the handler or the test.
